title: Nasdaq 100 Enters Correction Territory as AI Spending Fears and China's Chip Breakthrough Rattle Markets
excerpt: The tech-heavy index fell 10% from its June peak as a chip stock rout deepened on concerns over massive AI capital expenditure and reports of Chinese semiconductor advances.
body:
• The Nasdaq 100 fell 1.6% on Tuesday, officially entering correction territory after a 10% decline from its June peak
  • Chipmakers led the selloff, with Micron dropping 10%, AMD falling 8.4%, and Intel sliding 7% as investors questioned the returns on massive AI spending
  • China's CXMT soared 466% in its Shanghai debut to become mainland China's most valuable company at $487 billion, stoking fears of growing Chinese competition in semiconductors
  • Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's speech on Wednesday and upcoming big tech earnings could determine whether the selloff accelerates or stabilizes
  • South Korea's Kospi index plunged 11% as the chip rout spread globally, dragging down Samsung and SK Hynix

Markets in Turmoil

The Nasdaq 100 tumbled into correction territory on Tuesday as a deepening chip stock rout and mounting skepticism over the return on artificial intelligence investment sent technology shares sharply lower. The tech-heavy index fell 1.6%, breaching the 10% decline threshold from its June peak that formally marks a correction.

The broader market painted a starkly bifurcated picture. While the Nasdaq bled red, the Dow Jones Industrial Average surged more than 400 points, gaining 0.8%, as investors rotated out of technology and into other sectors. The S&P 500 dipped 0.2%, weighed down by its heavy tech weighting.

"Wednesday may be the most important day for markets in recent memory as Chair Warsh will have an opportunity to update investors on the prospects of a rate hike given rising oil prices, and big tech earnings may help shed light on whether or not we are finally seeing a return on investment for the massive amounts of AI spending taking place."

— Rick Gardner, Chief Investment Officer, RGA Investments

The AI Spending Question

At the heart of the selloff is a fundamental question: will the hundreds of billions of dollars being poured into artificial intelligence infrastructure actually generate adequate returns? So far this year, Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft have announced planned capital expenditures of as much as $205 billion, $200 billion, and $190 billion respectively — staggering sums that have left investors increasingly uneasy.

American chipmakers bore the brunt of the selling. Micron plunged 10%, AMD fell 8.4%, Intel dropped 7%, Broadcom slid 1.8%, and even Nvidia — the poster child of the AI boom — declined 1%. The once-sleepy memory chip business, which saw exponential growth as tech giants built out massive data centers, now faces questions about whether demand has been pulled too far forward.

The concerns are not purely domestic. A Reuters analysis found that several market warning signals have flared to levels close to crisis territory, with AI hyperscaler bond yields climbing faster than Treasury yields and the cost of hedging credit deterioration soaring.

China's Chip Breakthrough Adds Fuel

Compounding the AI spending anxiety, reports that China has begun mass-producing advanced chip-manufacturing machines sent shockwaves through global semiconductor markets. Chinese chipmaker CXMT soared a staggering 466% in its Shanghai stock market debut on Monday, rocketing to a $487 billion valuation and becoming the most valuable company in mainland China after just one day of trading.

The rout spread rapidly to Asia. South Korea's Kospi index plunged 11% as memory-chip giants SK Hynix and Samsung both slumped, with SK Hynix falling below its IPO price. Deutsche Bank analyst Jim Reid noted that "renewed worries over AI investment spending, and competition from cheaper Chinese companies, have triggered another selloff in global semiconductor stocks."

Meanwhile, Chinese AI firm Moonshot is reportedly seeking a $50 billion valuation in a new fundraising round after unveiling an open-source model with capabilities that rival those of Anthropic and OpenAI. A top White House official has accused the Beijing-based firm of stealing from Anthropic's technology to help build its latest model.

What Indian Investors Should Watch

For Indian diaspora investors with significant exposure to US technology stocks, the selloff carries direct portfolio implications. India's Nifty IT index, which tracks companies like Infosys, TCS, and Wipro that derive a majority of their revenue from US clients, could face pressure if the tech spending pullback extends to enterprise software budgets.

However, the rotation into non-tech sectors could benefit Indian conglomerates and companies in materials, energy, and financials that have US listings or significant American operations. The easing of oil prices — which fell after a pause in US-Iran hostilities — provides some relief for India's import-dependent economy.

What's Next

All eyes now turn to two critical events on Wednesday: Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's remarks on interest rates and a wave of big tech earnings reports. With margin debt at a record $1.5 trillion according to FINRA data, and the ratio of bullish to bearish positions on Nasdaq futures at a 17-year low, the next few sessions could prove pivotal. Investors will be watching whether the tech earnings season can provide the fundamental justification for the massive AI buildout — or whether this correction has further to run.
